Imagery Analyst - AI/ML Training Data| $20–60/hr | Labeling | QA

A team is looking for imagery specialists for a project centered on drone and maritime sensor imagery. You'll apply real-world expertise to help train next-generation AI systems, shaping how models learn, reason and perform. No prior AI experience is required; your domain knowledge is what matters.

Scope of Work:
• Review and refine machine-generated bounding boxes on still imagery from drone and maritime sensors, ensuring accuracy.
• Identify and annotate objects that AI models have missed.
• Label data consistently and in line with the provided guidelines.
• Deliver completed annotated images within a secure Navy environment.
• Maintain steady, reliable throughput of completed images.
• Transition to annotating video frames as the project evolves and its scope expands.
• Document and communicate ambiguous cases or guideline questions clearly, using strong written and verbal skills.

Preferred Qualifications:
• U.S. citizenship and the ability to obtain a DoD Common Access Card (CAC), or willingness to participate in the sponsorship process.
• Demonstrated attention to detail and consistency in repetitive tasks where accuracy is critical.
• Experience with data labeling, bounding-box annotation or similar data-preparation work.
• Familiarity with aerial, maritime or sensor-based imagery, especially daylight and thermal formats.
• A track record in high-volume, quality-controlled annotation environments; experience labeling data for robotics or autonomous systems is a plus.
• Comfort using dedicated labeling software and willingness to learn new applications.
• Strong written and verbal communication for reporting and clarifying labeling requirements.

"TCS Q2 Results 2026 LIVE: Net profit rises 4% QoQ to Rs 13,884 crore, IT firm declares dividend of Rs 12 per share"

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) reported its financial performance for the second quarter ended September 30, 2026. TCS delivered a stable performance driven by operational execution and deal conversions.

Earnings Deep Dive & Financial Analysis

Revenue Growth & Constant Currency Performance
TCS delivered constant currency (CC) revenue growth in the range of 0.5%–0.8% QoQ. On a year-on-year basis, reported rupee revenue surged 11.2% to ₹73,188 crore, boosted by favorable cross-currency movements as the Indian Rupee traded near ₹97 per USD. 

Operating Margins & Cost Management
Operating margins (EBIT) expanded sequentially to 24.3%. Margin resilience was driven by: 

Operational Efficiencies: Realignment of project delivery models and higher deployment of automation and Generative AI workflows.

Easing Wage Pressures: Stabilization of hiring costs and optimized sub-
contractor expenses.

Currency Tailwinds: Depreciating domestic currency against key client currencies (USD, EUR, GBP).

Capital Allocation & Shareholder Returns
Second Interim Dividend: The Board approved an interim payout of ₹12 per equity share.
Record Date: Fixed for Wednesday, October 14, 2026. 
Dividend Yield: Over the past four quarters, TCS has maintained a total payout ratio exceeding 80% of net income, offering an effective dividend yield of ~5.0%

Share Market Perspective & Valuation

YTD Underperformance & De-rating
Stock Performance: TCS shares traded around ₹2,136 on earnings day, down nearly 35% YTD from its 52-week high of ₹3,336.70. 
Factors Driving Sell-off: Broad-based tech headwinds, macro uncertainty, reduced discretionary spending in Western markets, and fears that AI productivity tools could compress traditional time-and-materials IT contracts.

Valuation Multiples
Price-to-Earnings (P/E): TCS currently trades at ~13.8x–14.0x FY27 estimated earnings, well below its 5-year historical average of 25x–28x.
Risk-Reward Balance: The stock's current valuation provides a solid margin of safety, backed by a ~5% dividend yield, stable operating cash flow, and zero net debt.

Summary Recommendation
TCS remains a defensive core holding. While revenue growth has moderated compared to previous cycles, the combination of 24%+ EBIT margins, strong order inflow ($9.5B–$10B), and 14x P/E valuation makes the stock attractive for long-term value and income investors.

Three in a row: Midlands hiring hits its fastest pace since November 2022 

The latest KPMG and REC UK Report on Midlands IT Jobs is out, and the key findings are:

• Permanent placements up again (index: 52.1). Only the North grew faster. 
• Temp billings rebounded strongly (53.8) after two months of decline, well ahead of the UK average 
• Permanent vacancies still falling (45.8), now 28 months in a row, but at the softest rate this year • Candidate availability keeps rising, with redundancies a big factor 
• Permanent starting salaries rose at the fastest pace since February, driven by competition for skilled people and senior hires 

Skills in Short Supply: 
Permanent: Software Developers, Data Engineers, Automation Testers
Contract: AI/ML Developers, Software Developers 

My Take: Fewer vacancies but more placements tells me employers have stopped sitting on roles and are finally committing. The ones moving now are securing people before the market tightens. 

And look at that skills list. Candidate availability is up, yet Software Developers appear in both the permanent and contract shortages. 

More CVs do not mean more of the right CVs. 

I see this every week. 

The volume is there; the quality takes proper qualifying to find. 

This is exactly why partnership matters. When a role goes out to five agencies at once, it becomes a race to send CVs first, not a search for the best person. 

Give one good recruiter exclusivity and a realistic timeframe, and they can actually do the job properly: understanding your team and culture, headhunting the people who aren't applying, and qualifying every candidate thoroughly before anyone lands in your inbox. 

You get a shorter, stronger shortlist, candidates who feel genuinely valued from the first conversation, and a far better chance of the right hire sticking around.

For IT professionals, salaries are moving again, especially at senior level. If you've been holding off because the market felt flat, that picture is starting to change. 

With the Autumn Budget around the corner, the next few months will tell us whether this is the start of a genuine recovery. I'm cautiously optimistic.

What are you seeing in your team or your job search? 
Is confidence coming back where you are?

Something happened recently that genuinely rattled me.

I came across a group of candidates who, on the surface, looked completely legitimate (and really rather good!).


Spoiler Alert ... They were not!


They had put together around 10 highly relevant CVs, with impressive experience at real companies — the kind of companies that would absolutely have hired for the roles they were applying for. Over phone calls they were able to articulate their experience with clarity, and I was confident there was a real person on the other side!

And then there were the passports. Real-looking photocopies of passports, complete with real-looking contact details from references that made everything seem even more credible. Seemed legit! 

But something still didn't sit quite right. How often do so many fantastic candidates, that are all available to start exactly when the contract begins, and are all looking for exactly the right rates? 

I asked to have a video call with them before their interviews. A real person turned up! This wasn't an AI scam! But they definitely weren't the person whose passport I'd been sent. And bizarrely, several of them appeared to be sitting in the same room as the person before? The same background. The same environment. 

This wasn't just someone exaggerating their experience on a CV. This was a coordinated attempt to create completely fictional candidate profiles — using real companies, convincing documentation and real people to get through the process. 

I've been in this industry for a decade. I've had my fair share of knock-backs. I've had moments where I've questioned myself, my judgement and whether I was good enough. I've had to work hard to build confidence in what I do. And if I'm honest, this really shook me! Not because I was fooled — thankfully, the checks caught it — but because it made me realise just how sophisticated this is becoming. 

We're often told to look out for AI-generated CVs, fake LinkedIn profiles and candidates who aren't quite what they seem. But what happens when the CV is built around real companies, the documentation looks genuine, the contact details appear legitimate, and there's an actual person sitting on the other side of the video call? 

I'd be really interested to hear from other recruiters, hiring managers and talent professionals: Have you come across anything like this? Does anyone know the agenda behind it all?

Buying an AI system from a vendor doesn’t make the risk theirs.

They may have built the model, but your company still decides where it sits in the workflow, what data it can access, which outputs people rely on, and what actions it is allowed to take.

That is usually where the more important risks show up.

A hiring tool becomes part of an employment decision. 

A claims model becomes part of a healthcare outcome.

 A customer-service agent starts collecting information, changing records, or acting on behalf of an employee.

The technology came from somewhere else. But the enterprise chose the use case, connected the data, and decided how much authority to give the system.

Customisation makes the boundary less clear again. Fine-tune the model, connect it to proprietary data, or use it for something it wasn’t originally designed to do, and more of the responsibility may shift towards you.

Contracts can divide responsibility. They can’t remove your responsibility for how the system is actually used.

For any third-party AI system, it helps to be clear on three things:
- what the vendor is responsible for
- what your company is responsible for
- what changes once the system is customised

The model may be outsourced, sure, but the deployment is still yours.

😴 😩 CAN’T BELIEVE WHAT MESSAGE I SAW IN MY INBOX YESTERDAY 😔

It was from a job seeker, but after our conversation, I realized something important:

She didn’t actually know what she was searching for.

I received a message in my LinkedIn inbox yesterday. I read it carefully and discovered that she was genuinely tired and frustrated with the job search process.

She reached out to me for cold-call coaching and guidance.

I responded and asked her a few questions. After a short conversation, I realized that she was trying to fix the wrong problem.

She believed that every problem a job seeker faces comes down to their CV/resume.

She had already paid several people to rewrite her resume. Unfortunately, some of them were only interested in taking her money.

Her last six resumes were already strong. Most of the changes she received were simply different templates and AI-rewritten sentences.

And this is the reason I’m sharing this.

There are many job seekers out there making the same mistake.

Sometimes, your resume isn't the real problem.

It could be your job-search strategy, positioning, networking, interview approach, target roles, or the way you're connecting with employers.

So before you spend more money fixing something that may not be broken, take a step back and identify the REAL gap.

If you're a job seeker and you're unsure what is holding you back, you can reach out to me.

I’m open to having a free coaching/advice chat or call to help you understand where the gap might be.

I’m not promising anyone a job.

What I can say is that I’ve built relationships with founders and professionals in my network, and I receive opportunities to help identify eligible candidates for roles and contracts.

Sometimes, getting closer to the right opportunity starts with understanding what you actually need to fix.

Thank you for reading. 🙏

As "a friend who is a little ahead", as Senior TA & HR Generalist at Groove Technology, I was lucky to work with many respected universities: University of Science (HCMUS), HCMC University of Technology and Education (HCMUTE), University of Economics HCMC (UEH), HCMC University of Economics and Finance (UEF), and Saigon University (SGU). Through workshops and mock interviews with Faculty/Club, I met many young talents, the future workforce of our job market. 
Workshop "Protecting Labor Rights in the IT Industry": in each session, I joined hundreds of students to look at the "gaps" that few people notice: labor contracts, social insurance, and tax. Many students couldn't realize the difference between contract types or thought social insurance only matters after many years of work, or didn't see the hidden risks that are easy to miss when starting a job. 
Besides the workshops, the mock interviews were also really useful: we practiced realistic interviews, shared direct feedback from a recruiter's point of view, and fixed common CV mistakes.Even with AI support, you still need to know how to adjust your CV yourself, right?? ^^
What I shared wasn't dry theory. It was my real experience and real lessons from my own career, made for future talents. With some fun icebreaker games, students felt free to ask questions and explore each topic with me.
For me, HR is not only about hiring the right people but It's also about helping young people start their careers with confidence: from presenting themselves to recruiters to understanding and protecting their own rights. 💖 
I am truly thankful for every opportunity on this journey, and for the trust from the universities and clubs. I hope every student starts their career with a strong "base" 🙌

Sometimes a higher price reduces fear instead of increasing it.

A higher quote can feel more reassuring when it comes with evidence and a process the buyer understands. The two prices in this design illustrate different buying contexts, not a rule that expensive work is better. Uncertainty falls when the client can see what the money covers and how progress will be evaluated.

Imagine comparing two unfamiliar providers. One sends a number; the other explains scope, shows a relevant example and names the review points. The second offer provides more information about what hiring will feel like, regardless of which fee is ultimately appropriate.

1. Put the outcome beside the price, in plain language.
2. Attach proof that resembles the buyer's actual situation.
3. Explain how feedback, delivery and approval will work.
4. State realistic limitations so confidence rests on a clear agreement.

You cannot make an unsupported offer credible by increasing its price. Build the supporting information first, then choose a price you can explain.

Which matters most when you hire: price, proof or process?

The Manchester Digital talent work makes grim reading if you're hiring senior.

Hardest roles to fill across the North West: cloud specialists, data engineers, AI and ML people, and engineering leadership. Data engineering gets called out as an acute shortage. The stack in demand is Python, Java, JavaScript, .NET Core and React, which won't surprise anybody who's hired here lately.

Two things in it worth pulling out.

First, companies are hiring in smaller targeted numbers instead of big pushes, and leaning on contract and consultancy to cover the gap. That matches what I'm seeing. Fewer twenty person builds, more carefully chosen threes and fours.

Second, and this is the one that costs people money: when a process drags, the good candidates are gone. Not slowed down. Gone. The shortage and the speed problem turn out to be the same problem wearing different clothes.

The data's from 2025 so it will have shifted, but nothing I've seen this year suggests it's shifted in a kinder direction.

70+ screens. 6 roles. 1 design system.

That was GridWage, an AI-powered Employer of Record platform. The hardest part wasn't the screen count.

It was making one product feel like one product to six very different people.

An employer running payroll. An employee applying for leave. HR, operations, vendors and admins, each expecting a different "home".

Before I drew a screen, I sat with the founders to understand payroll, compliance and global hiring. In payroll, a confusing screen can mean someone gets paid late.

So the architecture came first. Then 14 modules on top of it: payroll, onboarding, leave, contracts, compliance, the AI workspace and more.

The design system held it together. Auto layout, variables, tokens, interactive components, so a status or a table meant the same thing to an admin and an employee.

Then I worked on the frontend with the team in React, Next.js, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS.

That's where the system got tested. A variable in Figma is a promise. In code, it either holds up or it doesn't.

Now I design every component as if I'll be the one implementing it. Often, I am.

If you've designed one product for several roles, what's the one thing you refused to let change between them?

Yet many projects are still staffed as if one team should do it all. When the gaps show up, the usual fix is hiring a developer for a 3 or 6 month engagement.

𝐇𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐡:

1) A short-term hire needs weeks to understand the codebase, the domain, and the team
2) By the time they are productive, the contract is nearly over
3) Knowledge walks out the door when they leave
4) You pay for learning time, not delivery time

𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐰𝐚𝐲: 𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞.

Each partner brings depth, proven processes, and a team behind them, not just one individual.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐰𝐚𝐲:

1) Faster delivery, because experts are not learning on your budget
2) Better quality, because each piece is built by people who do it daily
3) Lower risk, because there is a team behind every deliverable
4) Knowledge stays in an organization, not with one contractor

This only works with the right mindset. Software companies often see each other as competitors. But in a market where projects are getting more complex every year, the smarter move is to partner on what we are strong at and be honest about what we are not.

I thought the best work of my life ended... Then I found Claude and realised i'm just getting started

At the start of the year I had no idea what I was doing next. I'd left my career-defining years behind.

I went from running operations at a £13M business to asking ChatGPT "who's hiring?"
We had an international customer base and a place on the Sunday Times 100 Fastest Growing Private Companies list in 2024, you can't blame me for thinking that this was the best work of my life. Then it was over.

Ok so what now? Who needs what I can offer? What business should I build next?

That's how I stumbled into AI. To fill the time, I started studying AI, videos, tutorials, a Google AI foundations certificate.

I was of course already using Claude and ChatGPT for forecasts, financials and better-sounding emails. But I used it the way us 90s kids used Ask Jeeves or MS Paint; feeding my curiosity and creativity but never to create something worth sharing.

I started pressure testing some of my ideas with Claude Code, vibe coded tools to make life easier apps to teach me stuff I wanted to learn and realised that I'd struck gold. I'm a natural problem solver. I can spot an issue and design a solution, no problem. The gap has always been access to the right tools and the time to execution. 

Now with Claude, Codex... whatever I can just build the right tools if I can't find them and my time to execution is instant. (The only thing holding me back are those damn limits)

One of my first projects was the bones of a creator economy tool. It reads contracts and briefs parses the data into detailed brand deal records inside a sort of CRM system, with invoicing, payment terms and deliverables tracking built in. We use it every week to manage the brand partnerships Ama works on.

Naval Ravikant, said in his Almanack that specific knowledge applied with leverage is what changes your life. My years in ops, supply chain and consulting are the knowledge. AI and code are the leverage, because both scale infinitely. 

I don't know about you but, that excites the hell out of me.

If you had to build one tool from what you already know, what would it be?

Randstad went through 35 million job postings from 2021 to 2026. The AI role that grew the fastest - AI trainers, up 281%. Estimates put the whole category at about $8.5B in annual revenue across 50+ companies, with most of it concentrated in four players.

Just to get a sense of the pace of growth: Mercor's gross run rate doubled to $2B in about four months this year. Handshake, which started as a college job board, built a business of nearly $1B in AI training in roughly a year. After Meta's 49% investment in Scale, a second wave of US companies grew up around RL environments, evaluations, and expert data.

Indian companies are emerging in this space, and they are growing fast. One well-documented example: Deccan AI, headquartered in the Bay Area but run largely out of Hyderabad, grew 10x in the past year. Beyond the funded names, plenty of Indian firms doing this work don’t appear on any startup tracker because many are profitable and have never needed to raise.

Look at who these platforms are hiring: professors, doctors, lawyers, consultants, accountants, tradesmen, translators. Part-time, remote, paid by the hour, usually in dollars. A growing share of that work is landing in India.

The logic is simple. The demand is there: frontier labs are spending billions a year on human data. The supply is there: India has one of the deepest pools of English-speaking doctors, engineers, CAs and STEM graduates, plus speakers of languages AI still struggles with. The economics work on both sides: expert trainers in India can earn in dollars by the hour, multiples of what the same skills pay locally, and still cost labs less than equivalent talent in the US. While the logic made sense to me a while back, I'm now seeing this across varied people in my network: bankers, investors, consultants, accountants, doctors, and many others.

My guess is this is already bigger than most people think. India may already have a sizeable AI export sector that nobody is counting.

My rough estimate is that India is currently earning $0.5–1B a year from this, between the workers doing it and the Indian firms organising them. That's about the size of India's tea exports. If the market grows around 30% a year and labs keep needing human experts rather than replacing them with synthetic data and AI graders, it could match India's coffee exports ($2B) by the end of the decade.

It's hard to see because of how it's structured: contract work, foreign clients, payments that land in personal accounts. But sectors that grow this quietly usually show up later in other places - growth in local incomes, upskilling across the workforce, higher AI adoption, growth in freelancing, and companies that eventually spin out of them. It's worth watching closely.
